lessons.title: What Makes a Crash a Crash

body.text: A crash is not defined by how far the market falls. It is defined by how fast it falls and how badly people panic on the way down. Depth hurts your portfolio. Speed breaks your nerve.

children.text: Every few years a headline screams that the market has crashed. Sometimes the Nifty is down 4% in a week. Sometimes it is down 38% in two months. The same word gets used for both, and that sloppiness costs investors money, because you cannot respond sensibly to an event you cannot even name. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and the maths to measure any fall, from 1929 on Wall Street to March 2020 on Dalal Street.
Correction, Bear Market, Crash: Three Different Animals

markDefs.definition: The percentage fall in the value of an index, stock or portfolio from its previous peak to a subsequent low. A move from 100 to 70 is a 30% drawdown.
Measured from the highest value reached (the peak) to the lowest value that follows it (the trough), before a new high is made.

children.text: Every fall is measured the same way: from the highest point to the lowest point that follows. That fall is called a
drawdown
, and the distance is measured
peak to trough
. What you call the fall depends on two things: how deep the drawdown is and how quickly it happens.

body.caption: How Market Professionals Label a Fall

cells: Nifty fell roughly 16% between late September 2024 and early March 2025
Months to years, often a slow grind
Nifty fell about 60% between January and October 2008
Days to a few weeks, sudden and violent
Nifty fell about 38% in roughly two months in early 2020, including a 13% single day drop on 23 March

body.text: None of these labels is an official definition. SEBI, NSE and BSE do not declare a correction or a bear market. The 10% and 20% lines are conventions used by analysts and the financial press. A crash can also be part of a bear market: March 2020 was both.

body.title: Name That Fall
body.question: The Nifty drifts down from 24,000 to 20,900 over five months, with no single day falling more than 2%. What is the most accurate label?
body.explanation: The fall is (24,000 minus 20,900) divided by 24,000, which is about 12.9%. That sits between 10% and 20%, and it happened slowly over months with no violent days. That is a textbook correction. It would only become a bear market below 19,200, the 20% line.

The Maths That Makes Crashes So Painful

markDefs.definition: The fact that a percentage loss requires a larger percentage gain to recover, because the gain is calculated on a smaller base. A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to break even.

children.text: Here is the part most investors never work out. Losses and gains are not symmetrical. If your portfolio falls 50%, a 50% gain does not bring you back. You need 100%. This is sometimes called
recovery asymmetry
, and it gets brutal as falls get deeper.

body.caption: The deeper the fall, the steeper the climb back, because every gain is calculated on a smaller base.

children.text: Try it on a 50% fall: 50 divided by 50, times 100, gives 100%. On a 20% fall: 20 divided by 80, times 100, gives 25%.

body.title: The Climb Back: Gain Needed After Each Size of Fall

body.label: The Nasdaq Lesson
body.context: That is why the Nasdaq Composite took until 2015 to get back to its March 2000 peak.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: If the Nifty falls 20% from its peak, it needs to rise ___% from the bottom just to get back to where it started.
body.explanation: 20 divided by (100 minus 20) equals 0.25, or 25%. For example, 25,000 falling 20% gives 20,000. Getting back to 25,000 needs a rise of 5,000 on a base of 20,000, which is 25%.

body.title: Your Turn: A COVID-Sized Hit
body.prompt: Priya had ₹10 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund in January 2020. Her holding fell 38%, in line with the index, to ₹6.2 lakh by 23 March. What percentage gain does she need from ₹6.2 lakh to get back to ₹10 lakh? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Gain needed = 38 divided by (100 minus 38), times 100 = 38 divided by 62, times 100, which is about 61.3%. Check: ₹6.2 lakh × 1.613 is about ₹10 lakh. A 38% fall needed a 61% rise to undo it, which is why "the market is only down 38%" understates how hard the road back looks from the bottom.

children.text: Depth vs Duration: Two Different Kinds of Pain

Two falls of similar size can feel completely different to live through. A fast crash tests your nerve for a few terrifying weeks. A slow bear market tests your patience for years, as every rally fails and hope drains away.

body.title: The Fast Crash vs The Slow Grind

columns.label: Fast Crash: Nifty, 2020
points: About 38% fall in roughly two months
Multiple days with falls of 5% or more, and a market-wide trading halt on 13 and 23 March
Panic peaks quickly, headlines are everywhere
Back to the old peak by November 2020
Main risk for investors: selling in terror near the bottom

columns.label: Slow Grind: Nasdaq, 2000 to 2002
points: About 78% fall spread over two and a half years
Several sharp rallies along the way that later failed
No single moment of panic, just steady erosion
Did not regain the 2000 peak until 2015
Main risk for investors: buying every dip in a company that never comes back

body.title: Why "25 Years to Recover" Overstates the Pain of 1929

children.text: The Dow did not close above its 1929 peak until 1954. That number is real, but it measures only the price index. Two things softened the blow for an investor who held on:
Dividends.

Price indices like the Dow and the Nifty 50 exclude dividends. An investor who reinvested dividends recovered years earlier than the price chart suggests. In India, NSE publishes a Nifty 50 Total Returns Index that includes dividends, precisely for this reason.
Falling prices.
The early 1930s saw deflation in the US, so each dollar bought more goods. In real terms, the loss was smaller than the headline fall.

The lesson is not that 1929 was mild. It was devastating, especially for the many investors who had bought with borrowed money and were wiped out long before any recovery. The point is to always ask what a statistic is actually measuring.

body.title: The WhatsApp Group Panic
body.scenario: It is a Tuesday in a turbulent year. Your Zerodha Console shows your portfolio down 27% from its peak. Most of your money is in three smallcap stocks you bought after a tip. Your family WhatsApp group is flooded with messages saying "the market has crashed, sell everything". You check the Nifty 50: it is down 9% from its own peak, spread over four months.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's vocabulary, describe what is actually happening to the market and to your portfolio. What is the first thing you should examine before doing anything?
body.modelAnswer: The market has not crashed. A 9% fall in the Nifty over four months does not even reach the 10% correction line, and it was slow, not sudden. Your portfolio, however, is in a 27% drawdown, which is bear market territory for your holdings specifically. The gap between the two numbers tells you the problem is concentrated in your own stock choices, not the broad market. A 27% fall also needs about a 37% gain to recover (27 divided by 73). Before doing anything, examine why those three smallcaps have fallen three times as much as the index: is it company-specific bad news, weak results, or just higher volatility? Check each one on Screener.in for debt levels, profit trends and promoter pledging. Decide based on the businesses, not on the WhatsApp group, whose use of the word crash is simply wrong here.

body.title: What Matters More?
body.question: Two investors both suffered a 40% drawdown. Investor A recovered in 9 months. Investor B took 6 years. Which statement is correct?
options: Both had the same experience because the drawdown was identical
Investor A's fall must have been smaller in rupee terms
Depth alone does not describe a crash; duration changes the real cost, including years of lost compounding
Investor B must have held riskier stocks
body.explanation: The same 40% drawdown needs the same 66.7% gain to recover, but Investor B spent six years just getting back to zero. Those are six years of compounding lost, and six years of temptation to give up and sell. That is why you always ask two questions about any fall: how deep, and how long.

cards.definition: The percentage fall from a previous peak to a subsequent low. It measures how much value was lost before a recovery began.
The measurement from the highest value reached to the lowest value that follows it, before a new high is made.
A fall of roughly 10% to 20% from a recent peak, usually over weeks to a few months.
A fall of 20% or more from a recent peak, often lasting months or years.
A sudden, sharp, double digit fall over days or a few weeks, usually driven by panic selling.
A loss needs a larger percentage gain to recover, because the gain is calculated on a smaller base. A 50% fall needs a 100% gain.

points: Every fall is measured peak to trough as a drawdown; the label depends on both depth and speed
By convention, a correction is a 10% to 20% fall, a bear market is 20% or more, and a crash is a sudden double digit fall over days or weeks. None of these is an official SEBI or exchange definition
History's biggest falls range from the Nifty's 38% COVID crash to the Dow's 89% collapse between 1929 and 1932
Losses and gains are asymmetric: a 20% fall needs a 25% gain, a 50% fall needs 100%, and a 78% fall needs about 353%
Duration matters as much as depth: the Nifty regained its 2020 peak within a year, while the Nasdaq took 15 years after 2000
